newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian envoy hopeful of Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Canadian envoy hopeful of Zaire talks.

text.p: The special envoy appointed by the United Nations to bring an end to the escalating crisis in Zaire said on Wednesday that while the task looked formidable he was confident he could at least get all sides to sit down and talk.

The United Nations announced on Tuesday that Canada's ambassador to Washington, Raymond Chretien, was appointed to help resolve the conflict that threatens to plunge Zaire and Rwanda into a full scale war.
"It's an extraordinarily difficult mission," Chretien, the nephew of Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, conceded to reporters.

But because he knows the area and knows many of the leaders in the region, he maintained he was confident he could at least get the sides to sit and talk about ending the conflict. Chretien, 54, was ambassador to Zaire, with joint accreditation to Rwanda, Burundi and Congo from 1978 to 1981. He has been Canada's ambassador in Washington since 1994.
"I am confident about establishing a frank dialogue with the leaders in the area to see what can be done," he said.
He hoped that some form of a peace convention could be held by mid-December in the region. But he said the first task was to try to arrange some kind of a ceasefire.

Fierce fighting has erupted in eastern Zaire between Tutsis who have lived in the area since the 18th century and Zaire troops. Zaire says Tutsi troops from neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi have joined in the fighting, which has been escalating with exchanges of artillery fire across the Zaire-Rwanda frontier.
Chretien was in Canada's largest city to meet Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy to discuss his mission.
Axworthy told reporters after the meeting that the crisis pointed to the need for new ways of resolving an explosion of regional conflicts around the world now that the Cold War was over.
He said Canada intended to play a new leadership role in getting the United Nations and other groups to respond more quickly when conflicts arise.
Axworthy announced a new US$7.4 million fund that would be used to help Canada move more quickly to help find new ways of resolving conflicts around the world.
